texto:
SemaBOX, a Nairobi podcast studio, today published the Creative Africa Intelligence Report 2026: Podcasting 2025/26, a valuation of 330 African podcast assets on YouTube and Spotify that concludes the content is commercially undervalued rather than underperforming. According to SemaBOX, the sample generated more than $0.9 million in advertising value at local rates and would have been worth more than $2.3 million at the rates paid in higher-income markets, a gap of roughly $1.4 million the report calls the "geography discount."
In Short
A podcast company in Kenya counted how much money ads on 330 African podcast episodes were worth, and found the same audiences would be worth about two and a half times more if they lived in places like the US or UK. That matters to advertisers and creators because the African shows got more likes and comments per view than shows in richer markets, yet the ads sold against them cost far less. The report's own numbers do not always agree with each other, so its headline figures are best read as an upper-end estimate from one company, not a measured market total.
What the report measured
The report was launched in Nairobi today in partnership with Baraza Media Lab, according to SemaBOX. Its subtitle is "Value created. Value returned." The full text sits on SemaBOX's website at semabox.africa/cair.
The sample covers 227 YouTube videos and 103 Spotify episodes. According to the report, the YouTube window ran from June 2025 to June 2026 and the Spotify window from June 2025 to July 2026; a footnote defines the overall period as 1 June 2025 to 31 July 2026, which is the basis for the "14-month" figure used throughout. Data came from the YouTube Data API v3 and Spotify chart extracts, according to the report's reference notes.
Two points about the sample shape every number that follows. First, it is not random. The report says the content was "selected and ranked using engagement scores," and it acknowledges that "its average performance is therefore unlikely to represent the average performance of the entire market." Second, the report deliberately applies "the upper end of each sourced rate range," so its valuations are described by SemaBOX as "the content's potential ceiling value, rather than conservative or typical-case estimates."
The arithmetic itself is simple. Content Value is views divided by 1,000, multiplied by an applied CPM. Creator Earnings are Content Value multiplied by a platform revenue share: 55% for YouTube and 50% for Spotify. The 55% figure matches the long-form share described when YouTube's monetization director walked through the YouTube Partner Program in October 2024.
The rates behind the geography discount
Everything in the report depends on a short table of CPM inputs, and SemaBOX is candid that several are weak. South Africa is assigned $10.00, the higher of two disagreeing sources, rated medium confidence. Nigeria gets $2.89, rated medium-high. Kenya gets $3.20 from a single source, rated low. Ghana, Egypt, Uganda, Tanzania and Senegal share a $1.80 fallback, described as the "high end of project's Sub-Saharan default range" and also rated low.
The comparator is a "Tier-1" blended CPM of $19.75, rated low-medium. A footnote shows how it was built: an average of US ($30), UK ($20), Australian ($18) and EU ($11) rates taken from VloggingPro, a creator-economy website. The press release describes the comparison as rates paid "in markets such as the United States, the United Kingdom and Australia," which leaves out the EU input that pulls the benchmark down.
Applied to the YouTube views, those inputs produce the country table at the centre of the report:
- South Africa: 34 assets, 26.8 million views, $268,356 applied value, $530,003 at Tier-1, a 1.98x multiple
- Nigeria Diaspora: 36 assets, 20.5 million views, $403,969 at both rates, because the segment is already priced at $19.75
- Nigeria: 27 assets, 14.9 million views, $43,205 applied, $295,261 at Tier-1, 6.83x
- Kenya: 42 assets, 9.8 million views, $31,316 applied, $193,281 at Tier-1, 6.17x
- Egypt, Ghana, Uganda, Tanzania and Senegal: 88 assets combined, 11.2 million views, each at 10.97x
The five-country cluster at 10.97x is an artefact of method, and the report says so plainly. "The identical result in those five markets should not be interpreted as evidence that their advertising markets perform identically," it states. "It is a consequence of using the same fallback rate where a reliable country-specific rate was unavailable." Senegal and Egypt are represented by two and three assets respectively.
The Nigeria Diaspora line deserves attention. By PPC Land's calculation from the report's own table, that single segment supplies about 44% of the entire $908,975 applied Content Value, because it is valued at the Tier-1 rate rather than a Nigerian one. South Africa has roughly 31% more views, the report notes, "but Nigeria Diaspora produces about 51% more Applied Content Value because its assumed CPM is almost twice as high." The report's attribution chapter explains why the category exists: a podcast can be African in its creators and subject matter while its account and audience sit elsewhere, and SemaBOX says it classified channels using stated identity, studio location, editorial focus and audience geography rather than YouTube's self-selected country field alone.
On Spotify, the 103 episodes are spread across Kenya (29), Nigeria (27), Ghana (25) and South Africa (22). The report lists 34.56 million "modeled streams," generating $141,928 in applied Content Value and $682,560 at Tier-1 parity, which it calls "a potential 5x revaluation." The stream counts are labelled as modelled and are round figures, such as 13,881,600 for Kenya, so they are estimates rather than platform-reported plays.
Engagement against price
The release leads with performance. According to SemaBOX, the YouTube sample recorded a weighted engagement rate of 2.75%, against a benchmark of 1.5% to 2.2% in higher-paying markets, meaning engagement was 25% to 83% higher. The report defines the measure as total likes plus comments divided by total views across the 227 YouTube assets. Ghana (3.31%) and Uganda (3.32%) posted the highest country-level rates despite small view totals.
Format is the second strand. More than 65% of the YouTube videos run between 60 and 120 minutes, compared with a "most common episode length" of 20 to 40 minutes in the comparator benchmark. More than 68% of the top-performing shows distribute in both video and audio; a footnote puts the figure at 68.2% of the 330-asset sample.
Then comes price. The report gives the sample's blended Content Value CPM as approximately $5.66 against $19.75, "~3.5x higher (~71% lower in Africa)." That is the figure behind this article's headline.
The report is careful about what engagement proves. "Comments, likes and shares show that audiences are responding to content. They do not reveal whether those responses are positive, whether viewers trust the host or whether an endorsement will influence a purchase," it says. "High engagement may reflect loyalty, debate, controversy or disagreement." Because the sample was ranked by engagement in the first place, a comparison with an unselected benchmark is also likely to flatter it, a limitation the report concedes in its market-size chapter.
The top of the YouTube ranking illustrates the classification problem. The highest-value entry in the report's "African YouTube Top 10" is an episode of Trevor Noah's podcast featuring John Oliver, released 15 January 2026, with 2.78 million views and a 121.7-minute runtime, filed under South Africa. It carries an asterisk marking it "borderline African-domiciled (diaspora or ownership-unverified)." Four of the ten entries carry that mark, including a BBC News Africa episode with a 0.30% engagement rate.
Where release and report disagree
Several figures do not reconcile, either between the press release and the report or within the report itself.
Two sets of headline totals
The executive summary states that the content generated $1,045,149 in Content Value, rising to $2,446,482 at higher-market rates, a gap of $1,401,333. It puts creators' modelled share at $567,735, or 54.3%, and platforms' at $477,413. Section 5.2, which describes "the revised 227-item YouTube sample," gives different totals: $908,974.55 applied, $2,326,709.42 at Tier-1, a difference of $1,417,734.87, with modelled Creator Earnings of $492,839.59. The press release uses the section 5.2 numbers. The country tables add up to the section 5.2 totals, which suggests the executive summary was not updated after the sample was revised.
Blended CPM
The report's $5.66 blended CPM does not follow from its own country table. By PPC Land's calculation, the YouTube table implies about $9.21 per thousand views ($767,046 across 83.2 million views); adding Spotify gives about $7.72. The ratio of applied to Tier-1 value in section 5.2 implies African pricing about 61% below the benchmark, not 71%. The $5.66 figure is close to the YouTube rate with the Nigeria Diaspora segment removed (about $5.78), but the report does not say that is how it was derived.
Multiples and growth rates
The release describes the discount as "about sevenfold in Nigeria and Kenya." The report's table gives 6.83x for Nigeria and 6.17x for Kenya. Elsewhere, the executive summary says monthly active listenership across African audio-streaming platforms "grew by an estimated 32% year on year," while both the release and a later section say audiences are growing "by approximately 20% - 28% a year." The two may measure different things, but the report does not explain the difference.
Jobs language
The executive summary says current earnings "could sustain approximately 352 full-time-equivalent creator livelihoods," rising to 890, and speaks of "sustained jobs." Chapter 7 of the same report says it "cannot yet estimate... the number of full-time-equivalent jobs they currently support" and describes 352 and 890 as income units of $100 a month, "a scenario measure, not an employment count." The press release uses the narrower "income-equivalents" wording.
Unfinished citation
One claim in the infrastructure chapter, that "an estimated 85% of digital-audio consumption in sub-Saharan Africa takes place over metered mobile-data networks," is followed in the published report by the placeholder "[source needed]."
Platform access
The access gap is starker than the pricing gap, according to the report. During the study period, Spotify's Partner Program required a legal address in one of 14 eligible markets, "No African country was on that list." For a creator whose only legal address was in Africa, the report says, "the Partner Program advertising payout available through this mechanism was $0." The report adds that, as of 12 October 2026, the programme is available in 19 markets, none African, and that Spotify has announced a further expansion from 20 October 2026 whose published list "still contains no African market."
The programme has widened steadily outside Africa. It launched on 2 January 2025 in the US, UK, Canada and Australia, reached Sweden, Denmark, Finland and Iceland in November 2025, and in January 2026 Spotify cut its eligibility thresholds by about 80%, lowering the engaged-audience requirement to 1,000 and the episode count to three. A month after launch, Spotify said creator payouts were up 300% year over year. None of those markets is in Africa.
The report also corrects its own Spotify model. The 50% creator share, it says, is "narrower than the model previously implied": Spotify pays an enrolled creator 50% of the revenue Spotify recognises when an ad it has monetised plays, which "is not a 50% share of all estimated Content Value, total advertiser expenditure or Premium video revenue." The Spotify Creator Earnings column is therefore a "theoretical creator allocation under platform parity."
YouTube is less restrictive. The release and executive summary say its Partner Program was available in 13 of Africa's 54 countries during the study period, citing Google Support. All eight African countries in the report's YouTube table are among them. Some creators respond to these limits by registering accounts in the US, UK or Australia, according to the report, which warns that "successful African content may be attributed to the country where an account is registered rather than the country where the creator lives and works."
From dollars to livelihoods
The livelihood calculation divides modelled creator allocations by $1,400, the value of a $100 monthly income across 14 months. The $100 boundary comes from the Africa Creator Economy Report 2.0, which, according to SemaBOX, found that about six in ten surveyed African creators earned less than that from their creative work. At applied rates, $492,839.59 equals about 352 such units; at Tier-1 parity, $1,245,562.18 equals about 890, "without a single additional view," according to the release.
The report lists its own limits: the allocations are not verified receipts, $100 is not a living wage, the calculation assumes equal distribution, and it deducts no production costs, taxes or fees. It also explains why it did not borrow the Oxford Economics method used in YouTube's impact studies. Dividing published GDP by FTE figures yields about $111,111 per FTE for the US in 2025 and about $2,073 for India in 2024, a calculation the report labels as its own. The US inputs match the Oxford Economics figures behind YouTube's 2025 US impact report: more than $60 billion in GDP and over 540,000 FTE jobs.
Sizing the market
SemaBOX does not adopt a single figure for the African podcast market. It lists published estimates of 350 million to 600 million for 2025/26 (the report does not state a currency for that row) and notes that the scope is unclear, including whether North Africa is covered. South Africa has the most substantial published valuation, at a reported $195.3 million, with projections of $1.35 billion by 2034. Estimates for Nigeria and West Africa range from $80 million to $130 million, and for Kenya and East Africa from $45 million to $75 million. The Middle East and Africa digital audio market is placed at $1.37 billion in 2024/25, rising to $7.99 billion by 2030, though the combined figure "does not show how much revenue comes from Africa rather than the Gulf states."
Its own cross-check models annual output. Using 8,000 to 12,000 open RSS feeds publishing 18 to 24 times a year and 15,000 to 25,000 YouTube channels publishing 20 to 30 times, it arrives at an undeduplicated range of 444,000 to 1,038,000 publications, with a midpoint illustration of 710,000. The model assumes South Africa, Nigeria, Kenya, Egypt and Ghana account for more than 80% of output and that about 65% of RSS feeds go inactive after their first ten episodes.
Direct sales dominate. According to the report, an estimated 74% of podcast advertising revenue in sub-Saharan Africa comes from host-read advertisements and sponsorships negotiated outside automated systems, a figure attributed to media buyer survey data from The Creative Brief Africa 2026. Average revenue per user is put at $0.45 to $1.20.
The infrastructure case
An investment chapter sets out what the report calls an illustrative mature-market scenario, with baseline figures it says "require verification" and targets that are "operating targets rather than forecast results." Average regional CPM would move from $0.50-$2.50 to $4.50-$8.50, a midpoint increase from $1.50 to $6.50, or about 4.3 times. The share of episode inventory carrying ads would rise from less than 15% to 65%. Creator payment periods would shrink from 60-90 days to weekly, and a regional ad operator would take a gross 20% to 30%.
The report identifies three barriers to wider use of server-side dynamic ad insertion: data costs and playback quality on metered mobile networks, the lack of reliable delivery measurement, and currency and payment friction. It names Atunwa Digital, which inserts targeted ads into podcasts and livestreamed radio through an AdsWizz integration, as one existing provider, but says such services "do not yet operate at the scale required." It also notes a structural limit: a regional company "could not independently insert or sell YouTube's platform-controlled advertising inventory without YouTube's authorisation." Longer YouTube videos can carry mid-roll breaks, the report observes, but delivery depends on advertiser demand, viewer location and creator settings.
Recommendations follow for each group. Brands and agencies are urged to add African podcasts to shortlists and test host-read campaigns against completed views, referral traffic and conversion. Investors are pointed at dynamic ad insertion, audience measurement, catalogue aggregation and creator payments, tested through pilots. YouTube and Spotify are asked to widen monetisation, including a phased Spotify Partner Program pilot in Kenya, Nigeria and South Africa, and to publish country-level indicators. Policymakers are asked for transparency standards on ad rates, fill rates and payouts.
SemaBOX is not a neutral observer of this market. Its website describes it as a Nairobi podcast studio and incubator active in six African countries with a creator network of more than 400 titles, and the report lists SemaBOX among the studios in the value chain it analyses.
What the founders said
"African creators are producing digital media that rivals global competitors in audience commitment and attention depth, yet they are not receiving the recognition or revenue they are due because of structural barriers," said Dan Aceda, Founder and CEO of SemaBOX, according to the release. "The geography discount is our biggest challenge, but it is also our greatest opportunity. It is a valuation gap, and for global advertisers, investors and ad-tech developers, closing it offers a rare entry point into a fast-growing digital audio market."
Eric Kinaga, Executive Director of Baraza Media Lab, framed the launch in institutional terms. "African stories deserve African agency. And African creativity deserves a fair return," he said. "SemaBOX is living proof of what happens when we take that responsibility seriously."
Why this matters for the marketing community
Podcast budgets are growing, and the question of where that money lands is becoming sharper. A VAB report covered in September projected podcasts would take 48% of US digital audio ad spend by 2030, from 42% in 2026, and found 88% of weekly podcast consumers reach shows through video platforms. The SemaBOX sample, dominated by long-form YouTube video, fits that pattern.
Geography already shapes podcast economics in markets PPC Land covers regularly. Audioboom's third-quarter update, reported on 15 October, noted that growing UK inventory as a share of its mix lowers blended yield, a smaller version of the same pricing gap SemaBOX describes. Measurement, meanwhile, remains the precondition for moving budgets: IAB Tech Lab finalised version 2.3 of its podcast counting rules on 29 September, extending them to video, and the SemaBOX report says smaller African services "may not yet have the measurement systems, independent verification or reporting history required by large advertisers."
What the report offers buyers is a ranked list of high-engagement shows and a set of country CPM inputs, several of them rated low confidence by SemaBOX itself. What it does not offer is outcome data. It contains no campaign results, conversion figures or brand-lift studies; its own section on testing concludes that "value for money" should be "demonstrated through campaign outcomes, not inferred from CPM or runtime alone." Is a 2.75% engagement rate on an engagement-selected sample evidence of underpricing, or of selection? The report leaves that for pilots to settle.

Summary
Who: SemaBOX, a Nairobi podcast studio and incubator, with launch partner Baraza Media Lab. SemaBOX founder and CEO Dan Aceda and Baraza Media Lab executive director Eric Kinaga are quoted. The report's findings concern African podcast creators, advertisers, investors, YouTube and Spotify.
What: The Creative Africa Intelligence Report 2026: Podcasting 2025/26 values 330 African podcast assets (227 YouTube videos, 103 Spotify episodes) at about $0.91 million in advertising value at local rates and $2.33 million at Tier-1 rates, a modelled "geography discount" of about $1.42 million. It reports a 2.75% weighted YouTube engagement rate against a 1.5%-2.2% benchmark and a blended CPM about 71% below the comparator. Its executive summary gives different totals ($1.05 million and $2.45 million), and its stated blended CPM does not reconcile with its country table.
When: Published today, 20 October 2026. The sample covers 1 June 2025 to 31 July 2026.
Where: Launched in Nairobi, Kenya. The sample spans South Africa, Nigeria, Kenya, Egypt, Ghana, Uganda, Tanzania, Senegal and a Nigerian diaspora segment.
Why: SemaBOX argues that African podcast content is underpriced rather than underperforming, and that limited access to YouTube and Spotify monetisation, weak ad infrastructure and payment friction keep value from reaching creators. It asks brands, investors, platforms and policymakers to test and fund changes, while acknowledging its estimates are upper-bound scenarios from an engagement-selected sample.
